matches.vattel: Every interpretation that leads to an absurdity, ought to be rejected; or, in other words, we should not give to any piece a meaning from which any absurd consequences would follow, but must interpret it in such a manner as to avoid absurdity. His wording ("author of the disposition", "the act", "had he been present") is the earlier translation's and stays closer to the French than the 1797 text. The judge's reading is right.

items.note: Adams quotes II.282's rule against absurd interpretation and adds, outside the marks, his own condensation of Vattel's next sentence ('On appelle absurde, non seulement ce qui est impossible physiquement, mais encore ce qui l'est moralement'), presumably aimed at the impossibility of obtaining stamps. items.note: Adams quotes Leonard's unnamed use of Vattel I.210 ('The best writers upon the law of nations tell us'), asks to be introduced to these writers, and argues a colony becomes part of the state only by contract or new law; the marks belong to Adams's quoting of Leonard and Vattel is never named, so verbatim rather than quotation, and the date is 6 March 1775, not February. Leonard drops 'a colony' and writes 'equal' for 'equally'; 'or mother country' comes from the English translation and is not in the French.

items.document: John Adams, Novanglus [No. VII], 'To the Inhabitants of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay', 6 March 1775, answering Massachusettensis of 9 January 1775; in Novanglus and Massachusettensis (Boston, 1819), Project Gutenberg text

items.note: Adams condenses Leonard's sentence to 'when a nation takes possession of a distant territory, that becomes a part of the state equally with its ancient possessions' in order to deny that free nations or the best writers warrant it; through Leonard it renders the whole first sentence of I.210, not only its last clause as the judge's Vattel span suggests. items.note: Leonard sets Vattel I.210, unnamed, as what 'the best writers upon the law of nations tell us', between 'The colonies are a part of the British empire' and the imperium in imperio argument, to conclude that the colonies are subject to Parliament. items.french: Lorsqu'une nation s'empare d'un pays éloigné , & y établit une colonie , ce pays , quoique séparé de l'établissement principal , fait naturellement partie de l'état ; tout comme ses anciennes possessions. Toutes les fois donc que les loix politiques ou les traités n'y apportent point de différence , tout ce qui se dit du territoire d'une nation doit s'entendre aussi de ses colonies.
items.note: The note, which opens on p. 109 with I.34 (V19), runs on into the whole of I.210 ('antient', 'ought also to extend') and signs it 'D' Vattel', backing the memorial's claim that the colonies are part of the state and that acts against the fundamental principles of the constitution are void. The first judge's reading is right.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Footnote to the 'Substance of a Memorial presented the House, in pursuance of the above Instructions; and by them voted to be transmitted to Jasper Mauduit, Esq; Agent for this Province', Massachusetts House of Representatives, 1764, 'drawn up by one of the House' (presumably Otis); appendix to James Otis, The Rights of the British Colonies Asserted and Proved (Boston, 1764)
items.own_or_quoted: footnote of the memorial as printed by Otis, quoting Vattel in the 1760 translation; the note continues with I.210 and is signed 'D' Vattel' on p. 110
items.french: Il se présente encore ici une question très - importante. Il appartient essentiellement à la société de faire des loix sur la maniere dont elle prétend être gouvernée , & sur la conduite des citoyens : ce pouvoir s'appelle puissance législative. La nation peut en confier l'exercice au prince , ou à une assemblée , ou à cette assemblée & au prince conjointement ; lesquels sont dès lors en droit de faire des loix nouvelles & d'abroger les anciennes. On demande si leur pouvoir s'étend jusques sur les loix fondamentales , s'ils peuvent changer la constitution de l'état. Les principes que nous avons posés nous conduisent certainement à décider que l'autorité de ces législateurs ne va pas si loin , & que les loix fondamentales doivent être sacrées pour eux , si la nation ne leur a pas donné très - expressément le pouvoir de les changer. Car la constitution de l'état doit être stable : & puisque la nation l'a premiérement établie , & qu'elle a ensuite confié la puissance législative à certaines personnes , les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission. On voit que la société a seulement voulu pourvoir à ce que l'état fut toujours muni de loix convenables aux conjonctures , & donner pour cet effet aux législateurs le pouvoir d'abroger les anciennes loix civiles & les loix politiques non fondamentales , & d'en faire de nouvelles ; mais rien ne conduit à penser qu'elle ait voulu soumettre sa constitution même à leur volonté.
items.note: The note, apparently keyed to 'acts against the fundamental principles of the British constitution are void', reproduces I.34 from 'A very important question here presents itself' to 'submit the constitution itself to their pleasure', so that Parliament cannot change the constitution under which the colonists hold their rights. The judge called it unnamed, but the same note runs straight on into I.210 and is signed 'D' Vattel', so quotation fits better than verbatim.

items.label: quotation
items.document: James Otis, The Rights of the British Colonies Asserted and Proved (Boston 1764; London reprint for J. Almon, 1765), footnote to the passage on Parliament voting the King absolute
items.own_or_quoted: author's own footnote, quoting Vattel in marks and closing with the citation "Mr. D' Vattel, B. 3. C. 10. sec. 201"
items.french: Quelques - uns ont osé avancer ce principe monstrueux , que le conquérant est maître absolu de sa conquête , qu'il peut en disposer comme de son propre, la traiter comme il lui plaît, suivant l'expression commune, traiter un état en pays conquis : & de-là ils tirent l'une des sources du gouvernement despotique. Laissons des gens qui traitent les hommes comme des effets commerçables , ou comme des bêtes de charge

source.locus: Droit de la guerre et de la paix, Liv. III ch. VIII § 1
source.label: divergence (severity 3)

items.note: Otis quotes III.201 at length in the 1760 London translation, from "But if the whole state be conquered" through "the state of war subsists" plus the sentence on a sovereign who would enslave a conquered people, to deny that Parliament could vote the King absolute; the judge's match is only the middle of a longer quotation that runs from p. 111 to p. 112. The French covers the sentence where Vattel calls the conqueror's absolute mastery a monstrous principle, against Wolff, JG §§ 870-871 (and Grotius III.8.1).

items.label: verbatim
items.document: Massachusetts House of Representatives, letter to the Earl of Shelburne, January 15, 1768 (one of the January 1768 letters attributed to Samuel Adams; the editor says authorship is not conclusively determined), Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 1
items.own_or_quoted: the House's own text; the reuse is attributed only to 'the greatest writers on the law of nature and nations'
items.french: Mais si le parlement délibéroit de faire un changement si considérable , & que la nation entiere gardât volontairement le silence , elle seroit censée approuver le fait de ses réprésentans
items.note: The House turns Vattel's rule that a nation voluntarily silent on a change of its constitution is deemed to approve it into a reason for protesting the Townshend duties, so that colonial silence is not read as consent. The letter is to Shelburne, dated January 15, 1768, not an unnamed peer.

items.label: close paraphrase
items.document: Massachusetts House of Representatives, letter to Lord Camden, January 29, 1768 (attributed to Samuel Adams, authorship not conclusively determined), Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 1
items.own_or_quoted: the House's own text
items.french: les grands changemens dans l'état étant des opérations délicates , pleines de dangers , & la fréquence des changemens nuisible en elle - même , un peuple doit être trèscirconspect sur cette matiere , & ne se porter jamais aux nouveautés , sans les raisons les plus pressantes , ou sans nécessité
items.note: The House calls the Mutiny Act's requisition on the colonies 'a great change; and in its nature delicate', not to be made 'without the most pressing reason, or an absolute necessity', applying Vattel's caution on constitutional change to Parliament. Only a phrase is verbatim, so close paraphrase fits better than verbatim; the letter is the Camden letter, which reuses I.36 a page later.

items.label: close paraphrase
items.document: Massachusetts House of Representatives, letter to Lord Camden, January 29, 1768 (attributed to Samuel Adams, authorship not conclusively determined), Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 1
items.own_or_quoted: the House's own text, closing paragraph of the letter
items.french: s'il s'éleve dans l'état des contestations sur les loix fondamentales , sur l'administration publique , sur les droits des différentes puissances qui y ont part , il appartient uniquement à la nation d'en juger & de les terminer conformément à sa constitution politique
items.note: The House drops Vattel's 'alone' and restates his rule that disputes on the public administration are for the nation to judge by its constitution, then says the end of the British constitution is liberty and appeals to Camden. The judge was right on the substance; the addressee is Lord Camden.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Vindex", Boston Gazette, January 21, 1771, on the trial of the soldiers for the Boston Massacre (the same article later answers Philanthrop), Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 2
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text; the sentence is set in quotation marks but not attributed
items.french: Une constitution admirable y met tout citoyen en état de concourir à cette grande fin , & répand par-tout cet esprit de vrai patriotisme , qui s'occupe avec zele du bien public.
items.note: Adams moves Vattel's praise of the English constitution to jury trial: 'constitution' becomes 'institution' and 'this great end' becomes 'the great end of society, the distributing justice', while 'a spirit of true patriotism, which is zealously employed for the publick welfare' keeps the older translation's wording. The marks show a quotation, but the 'great writer' named just before speaks to a different point, so Vattel is not named.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Vindex", Boston Gazette, January 21, 1771, part answering Philanthrop, Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 2
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text quoting Vattel in marks, introduced afterwards as 'the language of a very celebrated author' whom Philanthrop will accept as an authority
items.french: La constitution de l'état & ses loix sont la base de la tranquillité publique , le plus ferme appui de l'autorité politique & le gage de la liberté des citoyens. Mais cette constitution est un vain fantôme , & les meilleures loix sont inutiles , si on ne les observe pas religieusement. La nation doit donc veiller sans relâche à les faire également respecter & de ceux qui gouvernent , & du peuple destiné à obéir. Attaquer la constitution de l'état , violer ses loix , c'est un crime capital contre la société ; & si ceux qui s'en rendent coupables sont des personnes revêtues d'autorité , ils ajoutent au crime en lui - même , un perfide abus du pouvoir qui leur est confié. La nation doit constamment les réprimer avec toute la vigueur & la vigilance que demande l'importance du sujet.
items.note: Adams quotes I.30 against Philanthrop's call for subordination. He inserts 'and the true patriot will watch' and 'the people' to make the body of the people the guardian of the constitution, and he leaves the middle sentence on violating the laws as a capital crime outside the marks.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Vindex", Boston Gazette, January 21, 1771, closing paragraph of the answer to Philanthrop, Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 2
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text quoting Vattel in marks, unnamed (the 'very celebrated author' of p. 151)
items.french: c'est contre les attaques sourdes & lentes que la nation devroit être particuliérement en garde.
items.note: Adams ends the article with the rest of I.30. It is 'uncommon' for the constitution to be 'openly and boldly oppos'd'; he cites the maxim 'no less essential in politicks than in morals', principiis obsta; sudden force 'strikes the imagination'; and he quotes 'Important changes insensibly happen: It is against silent & slow attacks...' to warn that Philanthrop's principles open the way to despotism. Only the maxim principiis obsta has a row (a possible Pufendorf-Barbeyrac citation); the sentence on silent attacks has none.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Candidus", Boston Gazette, October 14, 1771, Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 2
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text quoting Vattel in marks, attributed to 'a celebrated writer, who thoroughly understood his subject'
items.french: Par les loix fondamentales de l'Angleterre , les deux chambres du parlement , de concert avec le roi , exercent la puissance législative. S'il prenoit envie aux deux chambres de se supprimer ellesmêmes , & de revêtir le roi de l'empire plein & absolu , certainement la nation ne le souffriroit pas.
items.note: Just before the quotation Adams paraphrases the end of I.34 ('if we are voluntarily silent... it will be consider'd as an approbation of the change'). He then quotes Vattel on the two houses, adding 'be so infatuated', and goes from there to the people's right to resist a minister who sets up his instructions to Hutchinson as laws. The judge's 'attrib.' and undated essay is the Candidus article of October 14, 1771.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Valerius Poplicola" (as headed in the edition), Boston Gazette, October 28, 1771, answering Hutchinson's History of Massachusetts Bay on the colonists' subjection to the parent state, Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 2
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text giving Vattel's words without marks but named in a footnote ('Mr. Vattel, law of nature and nations') as 'another distinguished writer' after Locke
items.french: Mais tout homme naît libre ; le fils d'un citoyen, parvenu à l'âge de raison, peut examiner s'il lui convient de se joindre à la société que sa naissance lui destine. S'il ne trouve point qu'il lui soit avantageux d'y rester, il est le maître de la quitter, en la dédommageant de ce qu'elle pourroit avoir fait en sa faveur ( * ), & en conservant pour elle, autant que ses nouveaux engagemens le lui permettront, les sentimens d'amour & de reconnoissance qu'il lui doit.
items.note: Adams sets Vattel beside Locke against Hutchinson's claim that allegiance is perpetual and unalienable, and he silently drops the condition that the emigrant compensate the society ('en la dédommageant...'). The words are covered only by Burlamaqui and Pufendorf-Barbeyrac rows. The free right to leave that they state is the point on which Vattel departs from Wolff, Inst. § 1019, which requires the superior's consent.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Valerius Poplicola" (as headed in the edition), Boston Gazette, October 28, 1771, answering Hutchinson's History, Writings of Samuel Adams vol. 2
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text quoting Vattel in marks ('He further says'), named in the footnote to the preceding sentence
items.french: Il est des cas dans lesquels un citoyen est absolument en droit, par des raisons prises du pacte même de la société politique, de renoncer à sa patrie & de l'abandonner.
items.note: Adams uses the absolute right to renounce one's country against Hutchinson's perpetual allegiance. He then paraphrases Vattel's third case, the sovereign or majority allowing only one religion, to say the Puritans left England lawfully (covered by Wolff JG § 153, shared argument, and a § 153 divergence). The quoted sentence itself has only a Pufendorf-Barbeyrac note row and is the point Vattel holds against Wolff, JG § 154.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Candidus", Boston Gazette, 27 January 1772, answering "Chronus" (The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2)
items.own_or_quoted: Adams's own text, quoting Vattel by name ("the great Vatei")
items.french: les tyrans seuls traiteront de séditieux ces citoyens courageux & fermes , qui exhortent le peuple à se garantir de l'oppression, à maintenir ses droits & ses privileges: un bon prince louera ces vertueux patriotes, pourvu que leur zele soit tempéré par la modération & la prudence. S'il aime la justice & son devoir, s'il aspire à la gloire immortelle & si pure d'être le pere de son peuple , qu'il se défie des suggestions intéressées d'un ministre qui lui peint comme des rebelles tous les citoyens qui ne ten-dent pas les mains à l'esclavage, qui refusent de plier sans murmure , sous les coups d'un pouvoir arbitraire.
items.note: Adams quotes Vattel to defend jealousy as a political virtue and the "patriots" Chronus derides, silently dropping Vattel's proviso that their zeal be tempered with moderation and prudence. His wording ("in vindication of their rights", "hold out their hands to chains", "suffer the strokes of arbitrary power") follows an earlier English translation closer to the French (tendent les mains à l'esclavage, sous les coups) than the 1797 text; the quotation sits on p. 323 only, not 322-323.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Samuel Adams, article signed "Candidus", Boston Gazette, 27 January 1772, answering "Chronus" (The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2)
items.own_or_quoted: Adams's own text, quoting Vattel by name ("says Vatel")
items.french: les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission. On voit que la société a seulement voulu pourvoir à ce que l'état fut toujours muni de loix convenables aux conjonctures , & donner pour cet effet aux législateurs le pouvoir d'abroger les anciennes loix civiles & les loix politiques non fondamentales , & d'en faire de nouvelles ; mais rien ne conduit à penser qu'elle ait voulu soumettre sa constitution même à leur volonté. Enfin , c'est de la constitution que ces législateurs tiennent leur pouvoir ; comment pourroient - ils la changer , sans détruire le fondement de leur autorité ?
items.note: Adams strings together three sentences of I.34 in marks to argue that, as Magna Charta declares the fundamental laws, Parliament cannot alter it and an act against it is void. The same article quotes the earlier part of I.34 (legislators' authority "does not extend so far", fundamental laws "sacred", constitution "fixed") just before and its England example just after, so the whole run on pp. 325-326 quotes nearly all of the section; the wording ("to their pleasure") is the earlier English translation.

items.label: close paraphrase
items.document: Samuel Adams, "The Rights of the Colonists" (report of the Boston Committee of Correspondence to the town meeting), November 1772, section "3d. The Rights of the Colonists as Subjects" (The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2)
items.own_or_quoted: own text of the report (Adams), with footnote "See Lock and Vatel"

items.note: Same passage as V33: Adams's "a body politick or civil society of men" follows the I.1 form ("un corps politique, ou une société d'hommes"), which restates this definition, so the reuse should be counted once, under I.1. The definition itself is Wolff's (Jus gentium § 9), here a close paraphrase.

items.label: close paraphrase
items.document: Samuel Adams, "The Rights of the Colonists" (report of the Boston Committee of Correspondence to the town meeting), November 1772, section "3d. The Rights of the Colonists as Subjects" (The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2)
items.own_or_quoted: own text of the report (Adams), with footnote "See Lock and Vatel"
items.french: un corps politique, ou une société d'hommes unis ensemble pour procurer leur avantage & leur sûreté , à forces réunies.
items.note: Adams opens the colonists' rights as subjects with Vattel's definition of the state, grafting Locke's "Common Wealth" and "civil society" onto it (hence the note "See Lock and Vatel") and rendering "à forces réunies" as "by means of their union", apparently the earlier English translation. The I.1 form fits better than Prelim.1 (V32), which it restates; behind both lies Wolff's definition of civitas (Jus gentium § 9).

items.label: quotation
items.document: Massachusetts House of Representatives to Governor Hutchinson, answer to his speech of 6 January, dated 26 January 1773 (drafted by Samuel Adams with committee; The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2; Massachusetts State Papers pp. 351-364)
items.own_or_quoted: own text of the House, quoting Vattel ("the celebrated author, whom your Excellency has quoted") without naming him
items.french: Il faut l'interpréter de maniere qu'il puisse avoir son effet
items.note: The House turns Vattel's rules of interpretation against the Governor: after quoting "the celebrated author" that no contracting party may interpret at pleasure (apparently II.265), it quotes II.283 so that the charter's grant of legislative power must be read to take effect, not be nullified by Parliament's reserved power. The judge's page (421) is wrong: the passage is on p. 411; no source row covers this sentence, though the rule in the sentences before it has Wolff, Institutiones § 804 behind it.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Massachusetts House of Representatives to Governor Hutchinson, answer to his speech of 6 January, dated 26 January 1773 (drafted by Samuel Adams with committee; The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2; Massachusetts State Papers pp. 351-364)
items.own_or_quoted: own text of the House, quoting Vattel ("the same author who is quoted by your Excellency") without naming him
items.french: l'autorité de ces législateurs ne va pas si loin , & que les loix fondamentales doivent être sacrées pour eux , si la nation ne leur a pas donné très - expressément le pouvoir de les changer. Car la constitution de l'état doit être stable : & puisque la nation l'a premiérement établie , & qu'elle a ensuite confié la puissance législative à certaines personnes , les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission.
items.note: The House quotes I.34 to argue that the fundamentals of the province's constitution are fixed in the charter, so no provincial acts referring to acts of Parliament can be taken as conceding Parliament's supreme authority. The date is 26 January 1773; the wording ("fixed", "trusted") is the earlier English translation.

items.label: close paraphrase
items.document: Massachusetts House of Representatives to Governor Hutchinson, 2 March 1773, reply to his speech of 16 February 1773 (The Writings of Samuel Adams, vol. 2; Massachusetts State Papers pp. 384-396)
items.own_or_quoted: own text of the House, recalling its earlier quotation of "a learned writer on the laws of nature and nations"
items.french: l'autorité de ces législateurs ne va pas si loin , & que les loix fondamentales doivent être sacrées pour eux , si la nation ne leur a pas donné très - expressément le pouvoir de les changer. Car la constitution de l'état doit être stable : & puisque la nation l'a premiérement établie , & qu'elle a ensuite confié la puissance législative à certaines personnes , les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission.
items.note: Complaining that the Governor has not answered "that great man", the House restates I.34 in Vattel's words without marks (the fundamentals "excepted from the commission of the Legislators" unless the people "in very express terms" gave the power), now applied to the General Assembly. The judge's date is wrong: this is the reply of 2 March 1773, on p. 452.

items.label: quotation
items.document: Oxenbridge Thacher, The Sentiments of a British American, pamphlet, Boston: Edes & Gill, 1764
items.own_or_quoted: author's own text, quoting Vattel by name ("It is observed by Vattel")
items.french: Heureuse constitution ! à laquelle on n'a pu parvenir tout d'un coup , qui a coûté , il est vrai , des ruisseaux de sang , mais que l'on n'a point achetée trop cher.
items.note: Thacher cites Vattel's praise of the English constitution to show the British are jealous of their liberties, and argues that the colonists share those rights, which the Sugar Act wounds; he swells Vattel's "rivers" (French "ruisseaux") into "seas" of blood. The judge named the wrong author: the pamphlet is by Oxenbridge Thacher, not James Thacher.
